markscheme: The electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei of the two bonded atoms **(A1)**

prompt: Which correctly compares the C–C, C=C and C≡C bonds?
options: C≡C is the longest and weakest
All three have the same length
C≡C is the shortest and strongest
markscheme: **D.** More shared pairs pull the nuclei closer and hold them more strongly: C≡C is the shortest and strongest.

prompt: Explain how a coordination bond forms in the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, and state how it compares with the other N–H bonds once formed.
markscheme: The lone pair on the nitrogen of NH₃ is donated to H⁺, so both shared electrons come from nitrogen **(A1)**; once formed it is identical to the other three N–H bonds **(A1)**

prompt: Predict the shape and bond angle of **(a)** NH₃, **(b)** H₂O, **(c)** BF₃, **(d)** CO₂.
markscheme:
**(a)** Trigonal pyramidal, about 107° (four electron domains, one lone pair) **(A1)**

**(b)** Bent, about 104.5° (two lone pairs) **(A1)**

**(c)** Trigonal planar, 120° **(A1)** **(d)** Linear, 180° **(A1)**

Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so they squeeze the bond angles below 109.5°.

prompt: Which bond is the most polar?
markscheme: **A.** Polarity increases with electronegativity difference: H–F has the largest (about 1.8).

prompt: Explain why CO₂ is non-polar although its bonds are polar, whereas H₂O is polar.
markscheme: Both contain polar bonds because O is more electronegative than C and H **(A1)**; CO₂ is linear, so the two bond dipoles cancel **(R1)**; H₂O is bent, so the dipoles do not cancel and there is a net dipole **(R1)**

prompt: Explain why graphite conducts electricity and is slippery, whereas diamond does not conduct and is very hard.
markscheme:
Diamond: each C is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid 3D network, with no delocalised electrons **(R1)**

Graphite: each C is bonded to three others in layers, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that can move and carry charge **(R1)**; the layers are held only by weak London forces, so they slide **(R1)**

prompt: Which substance has hydrogen bonding between its molecules?
markscheme: **C.** Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to N, O or F. Methanol has an O–H group; in CH₃OCH₃ and CH₃CHO the H atoms are bonded to C.

prompt: Butane (M = 58, bp −0.5 °C), propanone (M = 58, bp 56 °C) and propan-1-ol (M = 60, bp 97 °C) have similar molar masses. Explain the order of their boiling points.
markscheme:
Butane: non-polar, only London forces **(A1)**

Propanone: polar C=O, so dipole–dipole forces as well **(A1)**

Propan-1-ol: O–H allows hydrogen bonding, the strongest, so most energy is needed to separate the molecules **(A1)**

prompt:
In paper chromatography, a spot moves 2.4 cm while the solvent front moves 6.0 cm.

**(a)** Calculate the $R_f$ value. **[1]**

**(b)** Explain why components of a mixture separate. **[2]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $R_f=\dfrac{2.4}{6.0}=0.40$ **(A1)**

**(b)** Each component has different relative attractions to the stationary phase (paper/water) and the mobile phase (solvent) **(R1)**; those more attracted to the mobile phase travel further **(R1)**

prompt: Draw (describe) the resonance structures of the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻, and explain what this implies about its N–O bond lengths.
markscheme:
Three equivalent Lewis structures, each with one N=O and two N–O⁻ bonds, the double bond in a different position **(A1)**

The real ion is a hybrid with delocalised electrons **(R1)**: all three bonds are identical, intermediate in length between single and double bonds **(A1)**

prompt: Give two pieces of evidence that benzene does not contain three localised C=C bonds.
markscheme:
All six C–C bonds have the same length (140 pm), between single and double **(A1)**

Its enthalpy of hydrogenation is about 150 kJ mol⁻¹ less exothermic than three times that of cyclohexene, so it is more stable than the Kekulé structure **(A1)**

It undergoes substitution rather than addition reactions with bromine **(A1)**

prompt: Predict the shape and bond angle of **(a)** SF₆, **(b)** PCl₅, **(c)** XeF₄, **(d)** SF₄.
markscheme:
**(a)** Octahedral, 90° **(A1)** **(b)** Trigonal bipyramidal, 90° and 120° **(A1)**

**(c)** Square planar, 90° (6 domains, 2 lone pairs opposite) **(A1)** **(d)** Seesaw, about 102° and 173° (5 domains, 1 lone pair) **(A1)**

Elements in period 3 and below can exceed the octet because they are larger and have available d orbitals.

prompt: Two Lewis structures of N₂O are N=N=O and N≡N–O. Use formal charges to determine which is preferred.
markscheme:
Formal charge $=V-N-\tfrac B2$ **(M1)**

N=N=O: −1, +1, 0 **(A1)**; N≡N–O: 0, +1, −1 **(A1)**

Both have the same spread, but in N≡N–O the negative formal charge is on the more electronegative oxygen, so it is preferred **(R1)**

prompt: How many σ and π bonds are in a molecule of ethyne, HC≡CH?
markscheme: **B.** Each single bond is σ; a triple bond is one σ and two π. Two C–H σ + one C–C σ = 3σ, and 2π.

prompt: State the hybridization of carbon in **(a)** methane, **(b)** ethene, **(c)** ethyne, and relate it to the shape around the carbon.
markscheme: **(a)** sp³, tetrahedral **(A1)** **(b)** sp², trigonal planar (one unhybridised p orbital forms the π bond) **(A1)** **(c)** sp, linear (two p orbitals form two π bonds) **(A1)**
